description: On waking one reports 'I slept happily; I knew nothing' — taken as memory of an experience in deep sleep of bliss and of ignorance, witnessed by the self.
The knower lives with the body till prārabdha ends, the sense of agency gone, virtues arising spontaneously, and the realization unbroken in activity and absorption alike.

In nirvikalpa samādhi the distinction of knower, knowing and known dissolves and only the mode in the form of Brahman remains unmanifest, like salt dissolved in water; it differs from deep sleep, where no such mode is present.
In absorption a bliss is tasted which the meditator is liable to relish and cling to; the texts count this as an obstacle and prescribe non-attachment through discernment.
The jīvanmukta is graded by the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha's upper stages: at the fifth he rises from absorption by himself, at the sixth when roused by others, at the seventh not at all.
The recognition 'I am the tenth' is immediate and ends grief at once; mediate knowledge ('there is a tenth') gives only partial relief.
Inner target: a sound on closing the ears and a blue light between the eyes; outer target: colours of space seen in front of the nose, rays, golden light, a light above the head.
Successive voids: space without qualities, supreme space like darkness lit by stars, great space like the fire of dissolution, space of principles, space of the sun like crores of suns.
After death one recognizes oneself ('this I am') and one's world; another, bewildered by fire and choked by smoke, does not.

description: (Jain report) By the eightfold Mahānimitta Gosāla foretells gain and loss, pleasure and pain, life and death.
From firmness of contemplation comes the power of command (PKS 1.13).
The visualized drop at the nose tip is lost in emptiness when the mind is steady.
Burning longing and love-madness for Cennamallikārjuna, the husband without death or decay; the self wound in its own desires like the silkworm.
Akka Mahādēvi's union with the liṅga in the Kadaḷi forest of Śrīśaila.
Allama awakens on receiving the liṅga from the unblinking yogi Animiṣa in a buried shrine.
The sword passes through Allama's body as through empty space, where it rang off Gorakṣa's adamantine body.
In the mindless state the body is still as a log, sense-objects are not grasped, the breath stops, the mind neither sleeps nor wakes.
At the end of life Amitābha and the holy assembly appear before the one who held his name; he dies without confusion.
With the rule kept: knowledge in three months, sight of the gods in four, power equal to theirs in five, kaivalya in six.

Discrimination, awakening, contentment, joy, thrill, patience, calm, meditation, knowledge, festivity, passion, dispassion, bliss, trembling, swoon and disturbance are listed as forms of nature arising in the practitioner (AmŚ 26).
The layman Ānanda gained clairvoyance (avadhi-jñāna) of great range through his vows and stages; Gautama doubted that a layman could see so far and was told by Mahāvīra to ask his forgiveness.
The soul's longing for the Jina as its only beloved and husband, a love without beginning or end.
Brought as a bride to Śrīraṅgam, Āṇṭāḷ entered the image of Raṅganātha and was seen no more.
Āṇṭāḷ dreams her wedding to the Lord: the procession of a thousand elephants, the canopy, the rites, the circling of the fire.
Driven by a perverted mind of desire the intermediate being goes to the place of its birth, attracted to the parents' union; a hell-being goes head down.

The intermediate being is seen by beings of its own kind and by the pure divine eye; it moves with the swiftness of karmic power, has complete faculties, is unobstructed, cannot be turned back from its destination, and feeds on smells.
An incurable colic drove the Jain monk back to Śiva; on receiving the ash and singing, the pain left him (tradition's account).

The first of Mahādeva's five points: an arhat may have an impure emission through the temptation of others (deities) — affirmed by the Mahāsāṃghika side per Sarvāstivāda accounts, denied by the Theravāda (Kv 2.1) and the Sarvāstivāda.
Uncaused changes in complexion, voice, smell, taste, touch, the senses, mind, conduct and dreams that portend death.

Signs of Arjuna's despondency (viṣāda) on seeing his kin arrayed for battle, in his own words: his limbs give way, his mouth dries, his body trembles, his hair stands on end, the bow Gāṇḍīva slips from his hand, his skin burns, he cannot stand steady and his mind seems to whirl (1.28–30). The adverse omens he sees (1.31) are recorded separately (phn:bhagavad-gita-adverse-omens).
alt_description: At the sight of his kinsmen Arjuna's limbs fail, his mouth dries, his body trembles, his hair stands on end, the bow slips from his hand, his skin burns and his mind reels.

description: The bodhisattva cultivates the three doors of liberation even in dreams; a deed in a dream does not accumulate unless dwelt on after waking.
Signs of the irreversible bodhisattva: no doubt, no looking to other teachers, keeping the wholesome ways even in dreams, unmoved by Māra appearing as the Buddha.
During his austerities the bodhisatta felt violent winds, pains and burning in the body and became emaciated, yet the painful feelings did not overpower his mind; these did not lead to awakening.
Sleep/dream is 'neither alive nor dead', child of Yama; bad dreams are to be sent away.
Prāṇa stays awake, upright, among sleepers; none has heard of its sleeping.
Direct supersensory knowledge: clairvoyance of material things within a range (innate in gods and hell-beings, acquired by others) and, in restrained ascetics, direct knowledge of others' thoughts.
The liberated sage appears like a child, a madman, a dullard or a ghoul, fearless and untouched by desire.
'The Self alone is all; how can I say it is or is not? Wonder shines in me.'
Those who call Avalokiteśvara are freed from fire, water, robbers, weapons and bonds.
What is night for all beings, the self-controlled one is awake in; what beings are awake in is night for the seeing sage.

description: The guru, unable to bear the seeker's longing, comes and shows his own form; then the six supports, the fifty-one letters and all the principles are burnt, and the heart stands empty.
The Lord abides like the inner light of a ruby.
Tukārām appears to Bahiṇābāī in a dream and initiates her.
On hearing the brief teaching 'in the seen only the seen' Bāhiya's mind was freed at once from the effluents.

Bāhubali stood a year in body-abandonment until creepers climbed his limbs and ants built hills at his feet; omniscience came only when his last inner obstacle fell (pride, in the Śvetāmbara account; the thought of his brother's land, in the Digambara account).
Bāmākhepā saw Tārā in the Tārāpīṭh cremation ground and thereafter lived as her child (the tradition's account).
Taught the guṇasthānas by Rūpcand, Banārsīdās says his doubts ended and his mind became balanced, holding the pure self together with the stages of conduct.
After reading the Samayasāra, Banārsīdās and his friends held only to the ultimate standpoint and abandoned discipline — a state he later describes as a fall into one-sidedness.
At Svāmī Haridās's singing in Nidhivan the image of Bāṅke Bihārī appeared (tradition's account).
Near death from illness and austerities, Bankei coughs up a mass of black phlegm against a wall and at that moment realizes the Unborn.

In the bardo of becoming the deceased has a mental body with unobstructed movement and some clairvoyance, is blown by the winds of karma, sees the judgement of the Lord of Death, and is drawn to a womb.

In the bardo of dharmatā sounds, lights and rays arise; the peaceful deities with brilliant wisdom lights (beside dull lights of the six realms) and then the wrathful deities appear over successive days; all are the deceased's own projections.
The uncatchable Man is said to appear in the body at a certain time 'with the tide', like a fish swimming upstream (coded; summary only).
The unknown bird comes and goes in the cage; the Man comes near and slips away.
With the concentrated mind directed to knowledge and vision, one sees the body as material and consciousness bound up with it, like a thread strung through a clear beryl gem.
The bliss makes one stagger and dance like a drunkard (Pattirakiriyār 218).

Eighteen powers come to the yogin whose mind is fixed on the Lord; they are declared obstacles.
The eighteen (plus five) powers such as becoming minute or vast, hearing and seeing at a distance, entering another's body, dying at will, knowing others' minds.
Hair standing on end, melting heart, tears of joy, choked voice, weeping, laughing, singing and dancing without shame as signs of devotion that purifies.

description: 'Bliss, bliss — the bliss of no-thing', without clinging, the secret needing no accomplishment.
Reported (and rejected) view: in release the self's own bliss, overpowered in saṃsāra, becomes manifest and is experienced through the mind, which remains when the outer senses cease.

The released self has no cognition — its capacity to know remains but instruments and objects are absent — and no bliss; the state is like dreamless sleep except that saṃsāra does not resume (Pārthasārathi). The Prābhākaras likewise describe the released self as remaining in mere being.
One absorbed for three muhūrtas in the Bhāvanā contemplation attains identity with the deity, and what he intends comes about without effort (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
Bhīṣma holds his life-breaths until the sun's northern course; at death his self, restrained in all the openings, breaks through the crown of the head and rises to heaven.
Bhṛgu, deprived of breath by Varuṇa, sees in the quarters men cutting up and eating men and other retributions, explained as the fruits of acts in this world without the knowing Agnihotra.

Even the fleshly eye of the perfect Buddhas is supramundane and its qualities cannot be fathomed in an aeon; they possess five eyes.

The tradition's account of Caitanya's last years at Purī: divine madness in Rādhā's separation, wandering and fainting, incoherent speech of longing (citra-jalpa), alternating states of inner absorption, half-external and external consciousness.
At three the child was fed by Umā the milk of divine knowledge and at once sang the first hymn pointing to Śiva and Umā in the sky (tradition's account).

Entering other bodies, knowing others' minds, acting on things at will, divine sight and hearing, memory, radiance and invisibility at will — from concentration of the purified mind.

checks.note: All 1 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 8.6.3). It rests on 1 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

description: For one who knows the honey-doctrine the sun neither rises nor sets; for him it is always day.

checks.note: All 1 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (ChU 3.11.1-3). It rests on 1 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

description: The one who sees (thus) does not see death, nor sickness, nor sorrow; he sees all and obtains all.

description: Caraṇdās meets the sage Śukadeva in the forest and receives initiation from him.
The citta 'converges' (Thai: long) into stillness: body awareness fades and only the knowing remains, before withdrawing again.
Attachment (nikanti): subtle delight in the insight experiences — both an imperfection and a basis of imperfection; the meditator abandons his basic subject and sits enjoying it.
Illumination: light arising from insight, spreading over part of the body, a room, or far beyond; the meditator may take it for the path.
Knowledge sharp and quick, rapture of the five kinds, tranquillity of body and mind, and bliss suffusing the body arise in tender insight and are imperfections when grasped.
Strong resolution (faith), balanced exertion, firmly established assurance (mindfulness) and equanimity arise in tender insight and are imperfections when grasped.
Cūḍālā gained powers such as moving through the sky but hid them, using them only to help her husband; powers are distinguished from realization.
The old man appears, gives pān, touches the head and vanishes; seven years later appears again.
Sounds of the conch, thunder and waterfall heard in the brahmarandhra.
Meditation on the Lord, repeated until unbroken, attains the vividness of direct perception; this is how the meditator 'sees' the Lord before release.
At the eighth ground knowledge becomes effortless, like waking from a dream of crossing a river; the buddhas rouse him not to rest in peace.
At the tenth ground rays from all buddhas enter the bodhisattva's crown in consecration.
Signs in the breath, body, shadow and dreams are said to foretell the time of death, so that the practitioner may prepare with equanimity.
notes: Summary only; omen-lists not recorded.

description: At death a kamma, a kamma-sign (an object connected with a deed) or a destiny-sign (flames of hell, a mother's womb, celestial mansions and wish-fulfilling trees) appears at the mind door.
At the deathbed the dying may see signs of their sins or the lotus-dais and holy assembly; attendants record them and help repent the former until the latter appear (Shandao).
The state of the realised one 'whose condition, though in a body, is beyond the body' (Ātmasiddhi 142).
The gods see the Goddess's cosmic form with countless heads, eyes and feet and are terrified; it is seen only by her grace.
By contemplating the unities, the Samayins see the Goddess's form shining in the maṇipūra (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 7); after the great piercing she becomes manifest there (Bhāskararāya on LSN 37).
The dust-free, stainless eye of Dhamma arising in the hearer: 'whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation' — the sign of stream-entry (Koṇḍañña, Sāriputta).
A bright, clear sphere appears at the centre of the body, within which successive inner bodies are seen.
notes: No primary text read.

description: The body of the ascetic Dhanya, worn by fasting, is described limb by limb as dry and shrunken, praised by Mahāvīra (restricted theme: recorded as the text's description only).
In the first two dhyānas bodily ease comes from tranquillity; in the third the pleasure is mental; the fourth is unmoved, free of the eight disturbances.
The consecrated sacrificer lives as an embryo: in the hut-womb, wrapped in membranes, with clenched fists, until reborn at the final bath.

queries: local text at the stated ref
checks.note: AB 1.3 has 'punar vā etam ṛtvijo garbhaṃ kurvanti yaṃ dīkṣayanti …', with the hut as womb, the garment as membrane and the clenched fists. This rests on tea:aitareya-brahmana:1.3.

description: Only the dissolution of formations is seen, like the bursting of bubbles; with eight benefits including loss of fear of death.

At death: as earth dissolves into water the body becomes heavy and a mirage-like appearance arises; water into fire, the mouth dries and a smoke-like appearance; fire into wind, warmth withdraws and sparks like fireflies; wind into consciousness, the breath stops with a flickering lamp-like appearance; then white, red and black appearances and the clear light.
The omniscient's teaching issues as a single divine sound, without movement of the lips, understood by gods, humans and animals each in their own speech.
In concentration some perceive the world as finite, others as infinite, and take the perception as proof.
One fallen from the non-percipient gods recalls in concentration only the arising of perception, 'but no further', and concludes he arose without cause.
Some take the pleasure of the senses, or the first, second, third or fourth absorption, for supreme nibbāna here and now.

Ascetics who by ardent effort reach a concentration in which they recall up to a hundred thousand past lives, or many aeons, conclude that self and world are eternal. The text accepts the experience and rejects the conclusion: the Tathāgata knows where such grounds lead and what is beyond them.
At Rujing's words to a sleeping monk, the narrator (Dōgen in the Sōtō account) experiences body and mind dropping off, confirmed by Rujing.
Crossing a stream, Dongshan sees his reflection and awakens: 'it now is me; I now am not it'.

At the conception of a Tīrthaṅkara his mother sees fourteen great dreams (sixteen in Digambara accounts) — elephant, bull, lion, the goddess Śrī and the rest — which the dream-interpreters explain as signs of a son who will be a world-emperor or a Jina.

Direct vision of the Lord: most knowers see him within their own body; only gods, a hundred sages, a hundred kings, a hundred gandharvas and the like see him as all-pervading. The gods' liberation comes when Hari becomes directly perceived to them.
In deep sleep the soul, covered by tamas, rests in Hari as Prājña, neither desiring nor seeing; yet the witness perceives time even then.
Dreams are real, produced from latent impressions by the Lord as Taijasa within the mind.
At the knower's death the tip of the heart lights up, illumining the door by which he departs through the crown.

The liberated abide in various worlds up to the Milk Ocean, in sālokya, sārūpya, sāmīpya or sāyujya; those in sāyujya enter the Lord and come out; each class enjoys a hundredfold more bliss than the one below.
When the worshipper sits with the body straight, the suṣumnā shines, lit above the crown by the sun's rays, and in the heart-lotus Nārāyaṇa is contemplated.
notes: Stated as part of the contemplation in worship, not as a spontaneous sign.

description: The Turīya form of Viṣṇu at the dvādaśānta, not seen in ordinary life, is sometimes seen by the fully concentrated who have reached the sixteenth kalā and have direct vision.
When mindfulness of breathing has been developed, even one's last breaths are known as they cease, not unknown.
Distant hearing and sight, instant travel, perfection of speech, taking forms at will, invisibility, turning iron to gold, moving in the sky — to be regarded as obstacles.
Sweat, trembling, frog-like hopping, levitation in padmāsana; indifference to amount of food; little sleep and excreta; no worms, discharges, sweat or odour; great strength; a beautiful form.
When the channels are purified: lightness of body, radiance, increase of the digestive fire, slimness.
Women, captivated by the yogin's new beauty, seek union with him; yielding destroys bindu, shortens life and brings weakness.
When the wheel of Dhamma was set rolling, the cry of the gods rose to the Brahmā world, the ten-thousandfold world-system shook, and an immeasurable light appeared.
From the seventh month the embryo is conscious and remembers its hundreds of past births.
The image seen in the empty, not imagined, like a dream; the mind has neither existence nor non-existence in it.
Alone, secure, free from sorrow and vigilant, the mind wholly set on Rudra, he reaches the end of sufferings by the Lord's grace.
The Teacher and most witnesses are gone; the teaching is at its last breath and the stains are strong — a warning against heedlessness.
When the yogin, analysing with correct wisdom, sees no dharma arisen in the three times, he enters non-conceptual wisdom, pacifying all elaboration, and penetrates emptiness.
The mind looks on formations with equanimity, neither fearing nor delighting, like a man divorced from his wife who no longer cares what she does.
notes: Simile recalled.

description: Dream-bliss, the joys and 'experiences' taken for the ultimate — brass mistaken for gold.
Laziness, forgetting the object, laxity and excitement, non-application and over-application — the faults met in concentration.
Terror at the thought 'I am not, I will not be, nothing is mine' — the reaction of the childish to the teaching of definite goodness, which for the wise ends fear.
In a formless attainment Āḷāra Kālāma neither saw nor heard five hundred carts passing close by.
Joy, supreme joy, joy of cessation and innate joy as the drop moves through the centres; the innate is unchanging (summary; restricted domain).

First vision, direct perception of dharmatā (chos nyid mngon sum): lights, spheres (thig le) and fine luminous chains appear to the practitioner of direct crossing — the ground's display seen directly. (Restricted practice: description of the sign only.)
Second vision, increase of experience (nyams gong 'phel): the lights and spheres grow and spread, forms of deities begin to appear in them.

Third vision, awareness reaching full measure (rig pa tshad phebs): the complete maṇḍalas of the peaceful and wrathful deities and pure lands appear; ordinary perception of the body and world subsides.
Fourth vision, exhaustion of phenomena in dharmatā (chos nyid zad pa): the visions, the grasping body and the conceptual mind are exhausted into the ground; at death the rainbow body may result.
With burning coals heaped on his head, Gajasukumāla regarded his tormentor as a helper in shedding karma, kept pure meditation and attained liberation that night.
Inside Maitreya's tower Sudhana sees innumerable towers each containing all, with all of Maitreya's lives; it ends at a snap of Maitreya's fingers.
Long life without white hair, growing like the moon, radiance, a lion's strength; swift common attainments (restricted context).
The pain of death like countless scorpion stings, failing senses and consciousness, frothing at the mouth; the thumb-sized person leaves crying 'alas' and looks back at home.
The eight involuntary signs of ecstatic love — stupor, sweating, horripilation, faltering voice, trembling, change of colour, tears, fainting — graded from smouldering to supremely blazing.

Nine signs in one in whom bhāva has sprouted: forbearance, not wasting time, detachment, pridelessness, confident hope, longing, taste for chanting, attachment to describing his qualities, love for his abodes.
Warning: semblances of devotional emotion (reflected or shadow-like) can appear with tears and trembling in those whose hearts are impure or who seek other ends; such signs are not bhāva.
Sphūrti: vivid spontaneous manifestation of Kṛṣṇa or his play in the heart, reported in bhāva, distinguished from full direct vision.

Indrabhūti Gautama, sent away by Mahāvīra on his last night, learned of the nirvāṇa, grieved, reflected that the Jina had been without attachment, cut his own bond of affection and attained omniscience before dawn (tradition's account).
In devotional samādhi tears of bliss and thrilling of the hair arise, then a state beyond states, samādhi and manonmanī.

In the nocturnal bhrāmarī the sounds heard in the right ear are first like crickets, then flute, thunder, the hum of bees, bell, gong, trumpet, kettle-drum, mṛdaṅga, vīṇā and dundubhi; within the resonance of the unstruck sound is a light, within the light the mind, which dissolves there.

The powers claimed for the five element-concentrations: going to and from the heavens in this body, moving as swiftly as mind; not dying by earth, water, fire or wind; moving in the sky; for the space-concentration, the opening of the door of liberation.
By daily cleaning of the ear-openings the inner sound becomes manifest.

With khecarī, where the tongue meets the skull-cavity it tastes in turn salty, alkaline, bitter and astringent flavours, then butter, ghee, milk, curds, buttermilk, honey, grape-juice and nectar; hunger, thirst, swoon and sloth do not arise (the text's claims about a restricted practice).
In subtle meditation the awakened kuṇḍalinī goes out with the self through the eyes and roams the royal road, unseen because of her fickleness.
In mūrcchā, with the mind set between the brows and all objects abandoned, a swoon of the mind arises that gives happiness; joining the mind to the self, various blisses arise daily.
From breath-control: moving in the sky, removal of disease, awakening of śakti, manonmanī, bliss in the mind.
From the lowest breath-control sweat, from the middle trembling of the spine, from the highest leaving the ground.
By the practice of trāṭaka śāmbhavī surely arises; eye diseases do not occur and divine sight is given.

In yoni mudrā the practitioner, full of the power, delights in the supreme self with the sentiment of love, becomes full of bliss and one with Brahman — 'I am Brahman' — and non-dual samādhi arises; one established in it even once is in samādhi.

When the mind, knowing the truth of the self, ceases to imagine, it becomes no-mind (amanībhāva), grasping nothing for want of anything to grasp; this is described as peaceful, like nirvāṇa, the highest happiness.
Approaching the contactless (asparśa) state, yogins feel fear, 'seeing fear in the fearless'.
Sensations throughout the body — gross, solidified, painful at first, later subtle vibrations and a free flow in which the body is felt as dissolving (bhaṅga) — all observed with equanimity.
In separation the gopīs, absorbed in Kṛṣṇa, imitate his deeds and identify with him (tanmayatā).
Gorakṣa's body is said to be unbreakable — a sword rings off it — in the Vīraśaiva accounts of his meeting with Allama (reported by the opposing tradition).
notes: Reported by opponent source (Vīraśaiva Śūnyasampādane / Prabhuliṅgalīle).

description: (Jain report) In his last fever Gosāla drinks, sings, dances and salutes; his followers interpret these as the eight finalities; on the seventh night he recovers his senses and repents.
(Jain report) Gosāla's claim that the soul of Udāyi Kuṇḍiyāyaṇa had entered his body as the seventh of a series of reanimations.
(Jain report) Gosāla's fiery power burns two monks; hurled at Mahāvīra it circles him and enters Gosāla's own body, bringing fever and death within seven days.

Knowledge of the hidden and future, restlessness, intolerance and superhuman action; each class of seizer marked by its own behaviour (the god-seized pure, fragrant, truthful; the ancestor-seized offering rice-balls). Summary only.
The ground luminosity dawns at the moment of death like a clear, empty sky; recognized, it is the dharmakāya; unrecognized, consciousness faints and wakes into the bardo of dharmatā.
The body filled with nectar: the seed flows upward and the powers arise; the embodied one does not leave the body (GŚ 65–66).
At the heart centre the 'bull bound threefold' roars loudly (GŚ 60).
In breath-control: sweat in the lowest grade, trembling in the middle, rising up in the highest (GŚ 49).
In samādhi the yogī knows no smell, taste, form, touch or sound, neither self nor other, and is not devoured by time (GŚ 97–98).
Purification of the channels brings kindled fire, manifestation of the inner sound and health (GŚ-Briggs 101).
When mind enters the vajra of cessation, five signs arise in order: mirage, smoke, fireflies, a blazing lamp, and constant light like a cloudless sky.
Fruits of the limbs: blessing by all mantras, the five superknowledges, blessing by the bodhisattvas, entry of Vajrasattva, a halo of light, freedom from obscurations.
Signs of the prevailing guṇa: light of knowledge through all the gates of the body (sattva); greed, activity, restlessness and longing (rajas); darkness, inertia, negligence and delusion (tamas).
Hakuin's great doubt felt like being frozen in a sheet of ice; it shattered at the distant sound of a temple bell.
In the soft-butter method one feels the butter melting down through the body and the body soaked as in warm medicinal water.
Symptoms of Zen sickness: burning heat in the head and chest, ice-cold legs, ringing ears, timidity and fear, fatigue, night sweats and tears.

Effects accompanying the ten sounds: tingling, limbs 'breaking', fatigue, head shaking, dripping of the palate, drinking nectar, secret knowledge, supreme speech, invisibility and divine eye, becoming Brahman.
Ten inner sounds heard after long haṃsa-japa: ciṇī, ciñciṇī, bell, conch, lute, cymbal, flute, mṛdaṅga, bherī, thunder.

When the mind comes to rest one sees the self by the self and is content; one knows an endless happiness grasped by the intellect beyond the senses, is not shaken even by great sorrow, and attains the happiness of contact with Brahman.

alt_description: The state called yoga: the mind (citta) stilled (niruddha) by practice comes to rest; seeing the self by the self one is content in the self; one knows boundless (ātyantika) happiness grasped by the intellect and beyond the senses, and established in it does not waver from the truth; having gained it one counts no other gain greater, and is not shaken even by heavy sorrow; it is the disconnection from union with suffering.

description: Haridāsa Ṭhākura's death with the name on his lips and Caitanya's face before his eyes, followed by kīrtana with his body (tradition's account).
Hita Harivaṃśa receives his mantra from Rādhā herself (tradition's account).
Mekhalā and Kanakhalā cut off and offer their heads and are restored (the lives, from memory).
The mind's moods follow the petal of the heart lotus on which the jīva rests (virtue, sleep, cruelty, sin, play, movement, love, charity); at the junctions, disease.

For the precept-breaker of the lower-middle grade the fires of hell appear at death; on hearing of Amitābha's virtues they turn into a cool wind bearing flowers with transformation buddhas who welcome him.
Stages of mind known from practice: scattered and restless; coming-and-going with some bliss; clinging, steady and blissful; dissolved, very steady, with the highest bliss.
When the mind is left in indifference without being forced it becomes still of itself; in the no-mind state the yogin feels like one freed of a burden and experiences bliss beyond the senses.
notes: Hemacandra presents this as his own experience.

description: Hōnen dreamt of meeting Shandao, whose lower body was golden, who approved his spreading of the exclusive nenbutsu (the 'meeting of the two patriarchs').
Hōnen's samādhi record tells of visions in nenbutsu samādhi (1198–1206) of the Pure Land's ground, jewel trees, ponds and the Buddha's form, attained without contemplative effort through recitation.
At death, visions of welcoming buddhas or terrifying signs may appear; one should neither follow nor fear them.
Awakening at 'your original face', Huiming's whole body ran with sweat and he wept as he bowed.
At Huineng's death a strange fragrance filled the room, a white rainbow touched the earth, trees turned white; later a white light rose from the stūpa for three days.
On hearing 'produce a mind that abides nowhere', Huineng awakens that no dharma is apart from the self-nature and exclaims its five qualities.

Over thirty years Huiyuan saw the holy forms three times without speaking of it; at the end, rising from samādhi, he saw Amitābha filling space with transformation buddhas in his halo and the two bodhisattvas, and streams of light proclaiming suffering, emptiness, impermanence and no-self; told he would be born in seven days, he also saw deceased companions.
From holding bindu a pleasant fragrance arises in the yogin's body.
Signs of success in haṭha: slim body, bright face, distinct inner sound, very clear eyes, freedom from disease, control of bindu, kindled fire, purified channels.
At first ocean, thunder, kettledrum and cymbal sounds; in the middle drum, conch, bell and horn; at the end tinkling bells, flute, vīṇā and bee; the sounds become subtler as practice grows.
Claims for khecarī (restricted practice): no disease, death, sleep, hunger, thirst or swooning; not bound by karma nor afflicted by time; bindu does not fall; poison has no effect.
Apāna rises to the fire, the flame grows, heats prāṇa; the body's fire blazes; kuṇḍalinī, heated, wakes like a struck serpent, hisses, straightens and enters the channel of Brahman as if into a hole.
When mind and breath dissolve an indescribable bliss arises; breathing ceases, objects are not grasped, the yogin is motionless and changeless; the laya is known only to oneself, beyond speech.

For the practitioner of mahāmudrā nothing is wholesome or unwholesome; all tastes become tasteless and even terrible poison is digested like nectar; consumption, skin disease, constipation, gulma and indigestion disappear (the text's claims).
In mahāmudrā kuṇḍalinī straightens suddenly like a snake struck with a stick, and 'the state of death' arises (HYP 3.12).
In mahāvedha the breath leaves the two side channels and throbs in the middle; the union of moon, sun and fire arises and a death-like state (mṛtāvasthā) appears before the breath is released.
Beginning stage: the knot of Brahmā pierced, bliss from the void, tinkling sounds (unstruck) within; the body divine, radiant, fragrant, healthy, heart full.
Practised, the inner sound covers outer sound; within a fortnight the yogin overcomes all distraction and is happy; at first many loud sounds are heard, then subtler and subtler ones.
Ghaṭa stage: the united breath enters the middle, posture firm; the knot of Viṣṇu pierced, the sound of a kettledrum in the extreme void, indicating supreme bliss.
Niṣpatti: the knot of Rudra pierced, the breath at Śiva's seat; sounds of flute and vīṇā; the mind becomes one — rājayoga.
Paricaya stage: the sound of a drum (mardala); the breath in the great void, abode of all powers; natural bliss beyond the bliss of mind; no pain, age, disease, hunger or sleep.
When the channels are purified: slimness of body and radiance; holding the breath at will, kindled digestive fire, the inner sound manifest, health.
In the lowest (grade of breath-control) sweat, in the middle trembling, in the highest the breath reaches its place.

In samādhi the body is like a log and hears no conch or drum; no smell, taste, form, touch or sound, no self or other; the mind neither asleep nor awake, free of memory and forgetting; no cold or heat, pleasure or pain, honour or dishonour; in waking as if asleep, without breath.
After six months of the inverted practice wrinkles and grey hair are no longer seen; the digestive fire grows so that ample food is needed (the text's claims).
Improper breath-control brings hiccup, asthma, cough and pains of head, ears and eyes.
At initiation the guru contemplates a wave of light blazing like fire from the disciple's base to the aperture of Brahmā, burning away his sins and bonds (PKS 1.36).
At Kumano Hongū (1274) the deity appeared to Ippen and told him birth was settled for all as Namu Amida Butsu and to give the talismans to all.
Jaigīṣavya is seen by Asita Devala to arrive by yoga at distant places before him and to move among the worlds.
Janaka's exclamation of wonder on awakening: stainless, peaceful awareness beyond nature, long deceived by delusion; the world not other than the Self as waves are not other than water.
One whose mind in the new birth is joined with the pure (sattva) remembers former births — a 'rememberer of births'.
When Jayadeva hesitated to write that Kṛṣṇa asks for Rādhā's foot on his head, Kṛṣṇa himself, in Jayadeva's form, came while he bathed and wrote the line.

In each jhāna the body is pervaded: by rapture and bliss born of seclusion like bath-powder kneaded with water; by rapture and bliss born of concentration like a lake fed from a spring; by bliss without rapture like submerged lotuses; by pure bright mind like a man wrapped in white cloth.
The bodhisatta's recollection of entering the first jhāna as a child in the shade of a jambu tree, recognised as 'the path to awakening', and his realisation that he need not fear that pleasure.
Listening back to the hearing-nature on hearing crows and magpies, all sounds and discriminations become unobtainable, yet it is not empty space but 'bright and unobscured'.
The one liberated in life is free of 'I' and 'mine', equal-minded, untouched by the body's experiences; he may appear as child, madman or ghost.
Kuṇḍalinī seen as a young she-serpent bathed in saffron, coiled three and a half times, asleep facing downward, then rising to the heart where she hears the unstruck sound (Jñāneśvarī 6.221–275).
notes: Lineage given as Vārkarī; Jñāneśvar writes as a Nāth initiate (6.291).

description: As kuṇḍalinī rises the elements of the body are consumed; the yogī's body becomes light and radiant, as if made of light, and the separate self dissolves at the crown (summary).
On hearing of emptiness, great joy arising again and again, eyes filling with tears and body hair standing on end — the sign of one who has the seed of awakening and is a vessel for the teaching.
At Kabīr's death at Maghar, Hindus and Muslims disputing his body find only flowers under the shroud (the tradition's account).
Everywhere the Beloved's red; going to see it, the seer too turns red.
At the guru's one word the cloud of love rained and every limb was soaked.
Smoke, mirage, fireflies, lamp, flame, moon, sun, darkness, the digit and the great drop, then the universal image — clear light — seen with eyes closed or open, like a dream.
The liṅga's eye bled; the hunter gave his own eye, and the Lord's voice stopped him from giving the second.
Kapālakuṇḍalā arrives flying, saying she has drawn up the 'five nectars' through the rising order of the channels, having seen the self as Śiva in the heart-lotus - a hostile dramatist's portrayal.
The drunken Kāpālika declares that austerity gives the power to take any form - a satirist's portrayal.
Causeless devotion quickly dissolves the subtle body as digestive fire consumes food.
Melting love, then release of the image; the mind without support suddenly goes out like a flame; the self seen as one without division; the body no longer noticed.
At her prayer Śiva removed her beauty and gave her the form of a ghoul; she went to Kailāsa on her hands and was called 'Mother'.
At the Ghoshpara festival devotees are seized by bhāva (ecstatic possession), dance and weep; healing is sought at the tank and the pomegranate tree.
When the five senses of knowledge stand still together with the mind and the intellect does not stir — this is called the highest state.

checks.note: All 1 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (KU 2.3.10). It rests on 1 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

description: In the Kula rite arise inner bliss beyond mind and speech, possession by Bhairava and the vision of sameness everywhere; the self hidden by māyā is seen as a dark house by a lamp (restricted context).
Seven degrees of exhilaration from 'beginning' to 'beyond state'; the first five are waking, unmanā is dream, the equal state is deep sleep; knowing them one is liberated.
Meditation on the Goddess with the goddesses of speech makes one a poet of sweet speech (SL 17).
The teaching about brahman with respect to the gods: that which flashed in the lightning — 'ah!' — and made one blink — 'ah!'.

checks.note: All 1 Upaniṣad refs cited in the entry are located in the prepared segments (Kena 4.4). It rests on 1 teaching(s) text-located in this sweep, and its wording matches those passages.

description: Omniscience: knowledge of all substances in all their modes — past, present and future — at once, without senses or mind, with infinite perception, bliss and energy.

At the end of life an omniscient whose remaining karmas are unequal expands his soul's space-points to fill the universe and contracts them again within a few instants, equalising the karmas before liberation.
notes: From the karma literature (Gommaṭasāra, Karmagranthas; not yet anchored to a U35 teaching).

description: When excess and deficiency of karma are absent, the soul goes to Śakti; the sign of this descent is a distinctive devotion.
In one freed from bonds the sign is steadiness of disposition and unwavering adherence to the prescribed action; outward signs may be absent or inconstant.
In devotional singing the devotee's voice falters, the heart melts, he weeps again and again, sometimes laughs, and unabashed sings aloud and dances — such a devotee purifies the world.
The nectar-principle within the innate is seen throbbing, pure like a jewel, like a pearl or a firefly, sparkling like stars, white, red, black, smoky and yellow (KJN 14.95–96).
At the end of the twelve a throbbing garland of jewels is seen; the one who sees it is unstained by sin and merit (KJN 13.6; 14.90).

Successive attainments: people's affection, freedom from disease, poetry, mastery of speech, far hearing, leaving the ground, meeting the yoginīs, removal of old age, speed, many forms, peace (KJN 7.20–24).
With the mind fixed in the heart, samādhi with seizure and possession: the limbs revolve, cries arise (KJN 14.38–39).
In the 'great pervasion', the great sleep, one neither hears nor sees nor smells, fragrant or foul (KJN 17.16–17).

Practice on the root centre brings first trembling, then shaking; trembling of hands, feet and head; speech in many tongues; spontaneous mantras and seals; frog-like hopping; leaving the ground (KJN 14.16–19).
In the mind-less state the jīva, dissolved, is not roused even by drums, conches and flutes (KJN 14.85).
The adamantine body that does not dissolve even at the cosmic dissolution, Bhairava's own claim (KJN 15.22–26).
The disciple who received the command hastily and breaks the samayas becomes tāmasa, quarrelsome and fault-finding, and is 'dead while living'.
In the Kaurava court Kṛṣṇa laughs and from his lightning-like body emerge thumb-sized gods blazing like fire — Brahmā, Rudra, the Ādityas, Vasus, Maruts, Indra, yakṣas, gandharvas and rākṣasas.
Having gone above the crown, the high open space is seen (Kuṭampai 11).
notes: Checked in the local e-text; the second half-line is obscure.

description: By observing lamp-flames in the sixty-four-petalled lotus one sees throughout the body with divine sight (Kulānanda 6–7).
Absorbed in the Rāmāyaṇa recital, King Kulaśekhara took Rāma's battle as present and ordered his army to Rāma's aid.
When Tirumaḻicai asked the reclining Lord at Kuṭantai to rise and speak, the image began to rise and remains half-risen.
Kundakunda is said to have gone by supernatural power to the living Tīrthaṅkara Sīmandhara in Videha and to have heard the teaching directly (Digambara legend).

The roused kuṇḍalinī, like a serpent struck with a stick, enters the suṣumnā, pierces the three knots and six lotuses and unites with Śiva in the crown; the world is then seen to arise and dissolve falsely.

The Goddess's digit is seen as slender as a streak of lightning, made of sun, moon and fire, above the six lotuses, by those whose minds are cleansed of māyā; they hold waves of supreme bliss (SL 21; LSN 40).

The Goddess in the crown showers streams of nectar that drench the whole body before she returns to the base (LSN 39; SL 10); in the Samaya reading the nectar flows from her feet in the moon-disc of the crown (Lakṣmīdhara); in the morning routine it flows from the guru's feet (PKS 2.2).
Ascetics' attainments of a transformable body, a fiery body able to burn or bless, and a subtle projectable body sent to an omniscient to resolve a doubt.
Saying the nenbutsu without the dancing joy one expects and without wishing to go quickly to the Pure Land — shared by Shinran and taken as the working of blind passions, for which the vow was made.
By restraint of the breath Lal Ded lit the lamp of knowledge and saw the stainless form of consciousness.
The mind of the yogin who practises the yoga of the self is steady like a lamp that does not flicker in a windless place.

alt_description: The simile handed down for the yogin of restrained mind (yata-citta): a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker.

description: The nun Paṭācārā, drawing down the wick of her lamp, was liberated as the flame went out.

The freed soul manifests its own nature, its knowledge fully expanded; it experiences Brahman as inseparable from itself as his mode, shares his bliss and all powers except cosmic ones, and may take bodies at will or be without them.
Perception of light and vision of forms arising in concentration, which vanish when doubt, inattention, fear, elation and the other imperfections arise, and stabilise when these are abandoned.
Pratibhā (knowing the subtle, hidden, past, distant and future), śravaṇa (hearing all sounds), vārtā, darśana (divine sights), āsvāda (divine tastes), vedanā (divine touch).
Seeing peach blossoms after thirty years of seeking, Lingyun has no more doubt.
Linji awakens at Dayu's words about Huangbo's 'grandmotherly' kindness and exclaims there isn't much to Huangbo's Dharma.
A ray from the Buddha's ūrṇā lights eighteen thousand eastern worlds; flowers rain and the earth shakes in six ways — the sign that the Lotus will be taught.
One with deep faith in the Buddha's lifespan sees him teaching on the Vulture Peak and the world as a pure land.

The tradition's account of Madhva's feats as Vāyu's avatāra: eating a thousand plantains to meet a king's test, his toenail shining to give light, setting a huge rock in place, crossing the Gaṅgā without a boat, subduing a Yavana king with words, carrying the Kṛṣṇa image thirty youths could not lift.
notes: The tradition presents these as signs of his identity; no text checked here comments on powers as obstacles.

description: Endowed with these qualities he becomes a great chief of Mahādeva's troops, surpassing all paśus in lordship.
At the knowledge of arising and passing away, bright lights, rapture, calm, happiness, strong faith and effortless noting; meditators may think they have attained the path.
At path and fruition the objects and the noting mind cease; afterwards the meditator reviews the experience.
At the knowledge of re-observation strong pains, itching and restlessness may appear, with the wish to give up; they fade as noting matures into equanimity.
Repeating the Mahāvidyā mantras is promised eloquence, the eight powers and the six magical acts (Karpūrādistotra 1-5; Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.132-133).

For twelve and a half years Mahāvīra meditated in silence, naked after thirteen months, in empty houses, cremation grounds and under trees; in Lāḍha he was beaten and dogs were set on him; he took no medicine and fasted long, bearing all without anger.
Under a śāla tree by the Ṛjupālikā, squatting in the sun after a waterless fast, in pure meditation, the infinite and complete knowledge and perception (kevala) arose in him.
Piercing the darkness with Om as arrow, one sees brahman flashing like a whirling firebrand, sun-coloured, powerful, beyond darkness.

Five voids: dark space, space like the fire of dissolution, immeasurable light, space like the sun, and the indescribable blissful supreme space.
With the open gaze, signs appear: a star, a diamond mirror, the full moon's orb, nine gems, the midday sun, a flame.
Lights seen in the west: crystal, smoke, bindu, nāda, kalā, stars, fireflies, lamps, eyes, gold, gems — the form of the praṇava.
The fourth: neither inward- nor outward-knowing, not a mass of cognition, unseen, ungraspable, the stilling of the world, peaceful, auspicious, non-dual.

description: Śiva as a guru under a kuruntha tree at Tirupperunturai initiated the minister; the Tiruvācakam recalls being 'taken as his own' and the melting of the heart.
Fiery mantras awaken when the breath flows in the right channel, lunar ones in the left; when the breath flows in both, all mantras awaken and bear fruit.
In meditative absorption Mao Ziyuan awakened on hearing a crow's call: 'twenty years searching on paper ... suddenly hearing the crow I knew I had used my mind wrongly'.
At Vakkali's death the Buddha shows the monks a cloud of smoke moving in all directions: Māra searching for Vakkali's consciousness, which was unestablished.
For those who lack lineage and are proud of book-knowledge, the mantra's rays (marīci) turn against them through their breach of the samaya (YH 2.81).
First signs of yoga: lightness, health, gentleness, pleasant smell, scant excreta, radiance, clarity, pleasant voice; affection of others, fearlessness of creatures, indifference to heat and cold.
Prātibha (all learning shines forth), śrāvaṇa (hearing from a thousand yojanas), daiva (godlike sight), bhrama (unsupported wandering of mind), āvarta (knowledge whirling like a whirlpool).
stage: after the self has been seen

description: Mārkaṇḍeya's vision of the deluge and the infant on the banyan leaf, within whose body he saw the whole universe.
In the seven subtle dhāraṇās the yogin experiences himself as the subtle earth (losing smell), then water, fire, air, space, mind and intellect, abandoning each.
In the dissolution Mārkaṇḍeya sees a divine child on a banyan branch in the one ocean, is drawn into its mouth, and sees within its body the whole world.

The one beyond the guṇas neither hates their effects when present nor longs for them when absent, sits as one indifferent, and is the same in pleasure and pain, praise and blame, honour and dishonour.
At death (except for gods and hell-beings) the vital points are 'cut' by one of the elements, water and the others.

Ṛṣabha's mother Marudevī, weeping for her son, saw from elephant-back the splendour of his assembly, understood detachment, and attained omniscience and liberation at once — the first of this era (Śvetāmbara account).
The guru's forgetting and re-awakening: Matsyendra, entranced in the Kadalī kingdom, recognises himself again at Gorakṣa's drum-words (Gorakṣavijaya).
Reminded by Mahāvīra, Megha recalled his former birth as an elephant (jātismaraṇa) and was restored to steadiness in his vows.
Tears, trembling, hair on end, dancing and singing, the heart 'melting' (urukutal) as signs of grace — and the lament that it has not melted enough.
Swooned mercury (and breath) removes disease, 'dead' revives, bound gives sky-going — the texts' claim; RESTRICTED context.

stage: after death, as fruit of rites
description: Heaven is happiness (prīti) itself (Śabara); a verse cited by later Bhāṭṭas describes it as happiness unmixed with sorrow, not swallowed up afterwards, brought by longing.
A mind-made body drawn out of this body, complete in all its limbs, like a reed from its sheath, a sword from its scabbard, a snake from its slough.
When neither an entity nor its non-existence remains before the mind, having no other recourse the mind is pacified without object.
Minor rapture only raises the hairs on the body.
The poison sent by the Rāṇā becomes harmless; Mīrā drinks it laughing (tradition's account).

ref: he rī maiṃ to prema divānī
description: The madness and wound of love in separation: sleeplessness, pain no one else knows, healed only when the Lord becomes physician.
Momentary rapture comes and goes like flashes of lightning.
Powers shine forth pervading the universe like the sun's rays; no demon, titan or man can overpower the yogin, who blazes with the radiance of vision, action and breath.

In concentration objects are not seen apart from mental speech; everything appears as mind; first the object-side and then the subject-side of distraction falls away; non-conceptual wisdom free of duality arises.
In the kasiṇa and other concentrations, the bodhisattva's badness becomes slight; his body 'melts' (becomes pliant) moment by moment, and body and mind are filled with pliancy.
He perceives the unbounded light (appearance) of dharmas everywhere and sees signs that are not imagined, in purity.
When the seer sees the golden-coloured maker, the Lord, the person, the source of brahman, he shakes off merit and evil and attains supreme equality.

description: In the dark, cramped vestibule at Tirukkōvalūr the three first Āḻvārs felt a fourth, unseen presence pressing among them — the Lord — before the lamps of verse were lit.

Bliss (ānanda), leaping up (udbhava), trembling (kampa), sleep (nidrā) and whirling (ghūrṇi) - signs of immersion observed in the initiand; applied by Abhinavagupta to the āṇava practice of the breath (TĀ 5.101-111).

Signs that Rudra's power has descended: unwavering devotion to Rudra, success in mantra with immediate confirmation, control over beings, completion of undertakings, poetic power with sudden knowledge of all scriptures.
Naciketas, given to Death, stays three nights unfed in Death's house and receives three boons.

description: Absorbed in nāda the yogin lies like a dead man, body like a log, unaware of heat and cold, honour and dishonour; gaze, breath and mind steady without support.
Early loud sounds (ocean, clouds, kettledrum, waterfall), middle (mardala, bell, horn), late subtle (tinkling bells, flute, vīṇā, bee).

The ten forms of the unstruck sound in the Nādānusandhāna tract: ciṇī, ciñciṇī, ciri, conch, strings, a ringing, bronze cymbals, cloud, roaring water and the kettle-drum; the first nine are to be left, the tenth gives liberation.
The tradition's claim: the consultant's own leaf, written by a seer, is found through the thumb-impression and questions and read aloud with his name and those of his family.
When the channels are purified: lightness, radiance, strong digestive fire, leanness, breath held at will, the inner sound manifest, health.
Viṭṭhala eats the child Nāmdev's offering (tradition's account).
From birth Nammāḻvār neither cried nor fed and sat silent in the hollow of the tamarind tree at Kurukūr for sixteen years, absorbed in the Lord, until Madhurakavi's question drew his first words.
The tradition's account: Raṅganātha appeared as a child at the close of Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's exposition and recited a verse in his praise.
Nantaṉār entered the fire at Chidambaram and rose with the form of a sage wearing the sacred thread, then vanished into the sanctum.
Nārada in the White Island sees the white one-pointed devotees and receives a vision of Nārāyaṇa in universal form, a sight the Lord says even Brahmā has not had.
Blindfolded, Narahari feels Śiva's form in Viṭṭhala; unbound, he sees Viṭṭhala (tradition's account).
The tradition's account: after twelve thousand recitations of Madhurakavi's hymn in yogic absorption, Nāthamuni saw Nammāḻvār, who gave him the whole Prabandham and its meaning.
alt_description: After reciting the Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu twelve thousand times in yogic absorption at Kurukūr, Nāthamuni saw Nammāḻvār, who gave him the four thousand hymns and their meaning.

description: Knowing love, one becomes intoxicated, becomes still, becomes one who delights in the self; one desires, grieves over and hates nothing.
Love is indescribable, like a mute's tasting; increasing every moment, unbroken, subtlest, of the nature of experience; one sees, hears, speaks and thinks only of him.
The one-pointed devotees speak to one another with choked voices, bristling hair and tears.

With continuous voiced recitation samādhi is attained and the Buddha and holy assembly are seen clearly before one's eyes (Huaigan); 'great recitation sees a great buddha, small recitation a small buddha'.
The tradition's account of Nimbārka's name: he held the sun on a neem tree so that a guest ascetic could eat before sunset.
The mind placed, re-placed, stabilized, closely placed, tamed, pacified, fully pacified, made one-pointed and brought into equipoise on its object.
A stopping of all mind and mental factors, entered from the peak of existence and emerged from with a pure mind; the life faculty and heat remain.
In the thousand-petalled lotus the Lord is to be contemplated as a mountain is seen in a mirror; there Mahākālī, giver of nirvāṇa, dwells with the changeless one.

The three meditative experiences — bliss (bde ba), clarity (gsal ba) and non-thought (mi rtog pa) — arise as practice deepens; they are signs, not the goal, and grasped they lead into the desire, form and formless realms.
In dreamless deep sleep there is no affliction; later Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika explains the absence of cognition in deep sleep by the mind's resting in the channel purītat, out of contact with the skin-sense.
The Lord's eightfold lordship beginning with minuteness (aṇimā) is the fruit of His merit and concentration.
In practising samādhi, objects intrude by their force and hunger and similar urges drive one out; samādhi nonetheless arises from the continuing effect of previous practice.
One who, having contemplated outer objects and then the body within, dwells with a mind detached within and without is called liberated.
In loss of ojas one is fearful, weak, anxious, with afflicted senses, poor lustre, dejected, dry and emaciated.
With deep concentration a brilliant light of wisdom arises, by which the meditator sees the material groups and internal organs.
The empty, very empty, great empty and all-empty (clear light) arise in the completion stage.
The eighty natural conceptions that accompany the three appearances — 'night', 'day' and ignorance — move by the winds day and night.
Three states of love: unbearable longing for the Lord, direct vision of him, and love for which losing the vision would be unbearable.
The Goddess's worshipper, the bonds of the bound soul destroyed, tastes the rasa called the supreme Brahman (SL 99).

The love-sick girl (the Āḻvār as heroine) knows no sleep night or day, bails out her tears with her hands, joins her palms at the names of the conch and discus, and melts — as her mother describes her to the Lord of Śrīraṅgam.

As Pārśva meditated, the god Meghamālin (his old enemy Kamaṭha) sent storm and flood; the serpent-king Dharaṇendra and Padmāvatī, whom Pārśva had once saved from fire, sheltered him with their hoods — the scene of his images.
The Pāśupata siddhas at the Pāśupateśvara liṅga of Prabhāsa went to Śiva's abode in this very body (Purāṇic account).

stage: yoga arising (from the first stage on)
description: Seeing, hearing, thinking and knowing at a distance, omniscience, swiftness of mind, taking forms at will and acting without organs arise for the practitioner in whom yoga has arisen.

All become subject to him and he to none; he enters all and none enters him; he can slay all and none can slay him; he is fearless, imperishable, unaging, deathless and moves unobstructed everywhere (Kauṇḍinya: the eight marks of perfection).
In the tradition, at Tiruvoṟṟiyūr Paṭṭiṉattār had boys cover him with a basket; when it was lifted he had vanished and a liṅga stood in his place.
notes: The tradition's account (hagiography), not a verse of the songs.

description: In the tradition, when Paṭṭiṉattār was condemned to the stake at Ujjain the stake burst into flame.
At the peak of perception the monk thinks that intending and willing would be worse for him, so neither intends nor wills; those perceptions cease and others do not arise: he touches cessation.
Pervading rapture suffuses the whole body like a filled bladder or a cave flooded by water; it is the rapture of absorption.
By the light of the others' lamps Pēyāḻvār saw Śrī, the golden form, the sun-like hue, the discus and the conch in the ocean-hued Lord.
Samādhi that remains in all activity; lordship over the circle of the deities of one's own consciousness.

Signs of success in the training of transference: swelling, tenderness or a small opening at the crown, lymph or blood appearing there, into which a blade of kuśa grass can be inserted. (Restricted practice: sign only.)
In gradual death the mind ceases at the feet, the navel or the heart, according as the dying one goes to lower destinies, to the human state, or to the gods (arhats at the heart).
After six months of constant yoga the powers arise in abundance - gradually, one after another, like a needle piercing a stack of lotus petals in succession.
Prahlāda weeping, laughing, singing, crying out, dancing, imitating the Lord, and sitting silent with hair on end and tearful half-closed eyes.
Prahlāda, having realized the Self, remained in samādhi for ages until Viṣṇu roused him with the conch.
For one who contemplates 'I am you', the fire of the great dissolution itself waves lights before him (SL 96).
Forcible restraint of the breath brings pain, and the pain disturbs the mind (Hemacandra's warning against making breath-control a path).
Breath-control is graded by its signs: sweat (lowest), trembling (middle), rising of the body (highest).
In dream the mind experiences its greatness, seeing again the seen and unseen, heard and unheard; overcome by light (tejas) it sees no dreams, and happiness arises in the body.

description: The sentence's meaning flashes as a single intuition that cannot be described even by the one who has it.
Amitābha seen face to face in samādhi or in a dream, known as mind-made.

Becoming many and one, appearing and vanishing, passing through walls, diving into earth, walking on water, flying cross-legged, touching sun and moon, wielding mastery up to the Brahmā world; the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, past lives, the divine eye.
Signs of purification in Vajrasattva practice: dreams of bathing, of vomiting bad food, of discharging pus and blood, of wearing white clothes, of flying or of the sun and moon rising.

What is cultivated to culmination appears vividly as if present — the yogin's vision of the truths, but also the lover's, the grieving and the frightened person's visions of absent things, and the foulness and earth meditations.
Rādhā in separation: the bed of flowers burns her, moonlight is fire, she draws his image and wastes away, as her friend tells Kṛṣṇa.
At an advanced stage the citta becomes radiant and seemingly wondrous; Ajahn Maha Boowa describes this radiance as the last seat of ignorance.
Devotees hold that Rāghavendra, who entered his brindāvana alive, remains present at Mantrālaya and answers prayers.
notes: Living devotional belief; no textual source checked.

description: At the death of one who attains the rainbow body the corpse shrinks over days, rainbows and lights appear, and at the end only hair and nails remain (or nothing, for the great transference).
The tradition's account that Śrīmad Rājacandra remembered former lives from the age of seven (jātismaraṇa), later accompanied by self-realisation described in his letters.
notes: The tradition's account; not anchored to a U35 teaching (see trm:jatismarana, U34).

description: To the yogin constantly practising samādhi, with senses withdrawn and the six inner enemies conquered, Rāma is always visible.
The Mother came to Rāmprasād in the form of his daughter and helped him mend a fence (the tradition's account).
Aesthetic rapture: a relish in which consciousness, freed from personal limits and other objects, rests in itself as bliss and wonder — 'the twin of tasting Brahman'.
The conscious light between the eyebrows, illuminating the world like fire, lightning or sun: supreme bliss, free of conception and affliction, peaceful, self-known.
Those who attained brahmanhood live on, free of passion and hatred, same toward all, their bodies shining, joyful, endowed with the subtle powers (aṇimā and the rest) — the texts' claim.
Long life, memory, intelligence, health, youth, lustre, complexion and voice, strength of body and senses, success of speech, respect and radiance.
The Gaṅgā appears in Ravidās's leather-soaking bowl (legend behind 'man cangā to kaṭhautī meṃ gaṅgā').
Relics (sku gdung, ring bsrel) of various colours and kinds found in the cremation of accomplished practitioners, with lights and sounds, as signs of their realization (Blazing Relics tantra).
The seers 'saw' the hymns when Brahman the self-existent came upon them in austerity; they had direct vision of dharma.

description: Dwelling in the cremation ground and living on what comes, he attains union with Rudra - direct conjunction with him (Kauṇḍinya).
To the doubter who asks 'who has seen Indra?' Indra answers 'here I am, singer, look at me'.
Ecstatic with munihood the sages mount the winds while mortals see only their bodies; the muni flies through the air seeing all forms and knows the intent of beings.
Under soma the speaker feels the five peoples as a mote, both worlds not equal to one of his wings, himself 'great of the great', raised to the clouds.
Rising from the darkness, seeing the higher light, the worshippers come to the highest light, Sūrya.
A fixed light set to be seen; 'my ears fly open, my eye, this light set in the heart; my mind roams far; what shall I say, what shall I think?'
The seers, searching in their hearts with wisdom, found the bond of being in non-being.
The wise see with heart and mind the bird anointed with the asura's māyā.
'I do not know what I am like; secret, bound, I wander with my mind' — until the first-born of ṛta comes and the seer receives a share of speech.
Soma produces bliss (ānanda); the immortal world is where joys, delights and the desires of desire are attained.
After drinking soma: 'we have become immortal, we have gone to the light, we have found the gods; what can hostility do to us now?'
Speech is not seen by one who sees nor heard by one who hears, but reveals her body to another like a loving bride.
Speech speaks as the one who moves with all the gods, through whom all eat, see and breathe, who has become 'so great, beyond heaven and earth'.
The seer speaks as Manu, the Sun, Kakṣīvant and Uśanas, and says he knew in the womb all the births of the gods.
Vasiṣṭha sails with Varuṇa on the sea, swinging for joy, and is made a seer by him.
The rivers stop and lower their waters at the seer's words.
In 1117, in samādhi, Amida appeared to Ryōnin and revealed the verse of the interfusing nenbutsu.
In sahaj samādhi the eyes stay open and the Lord's form is seen everywhere; the state grows day by day.
Samantabhadra appears on a six-tusked white elephant to those who recite the Lotus and gives them dhāraṇīs.
The gods raise a circular assembly of concentric walls and gateways in which beings of every kind sit in twelve assemblies, animals without enmity, while the Jina appears to face all four directions.
In concentration, deep sleep and liberation puruṣa has the form of Brahman — with seed in the first two, the seed destroyed in liberation.
From repeated practice of the principles the knowledge 'I am not, (nothing is) mine, not I' arises — complete, pure because free of error, and single.
After perfect knowledge the body continues by the momentum of impressions, as a potter's wheel keeps turning.
Prakṛti, having shown herself, withdraws like a dancer and, knowing 'I have been seen', does not come into view again; puruṣa sees her like a spectator, at ease, and remains indifferent.
Powers from concentrations: knowledge of the worlds, of past and future, of others' minds; freedom from hunger; steadiness; vision of siddhas; moving in space.
Through Vyāsa's gift Sañjaya sees and knows everything in the battle, in open or in secret, even thoughts.
Jñāneśvar sits in meditation, closes his eyes and is sealed in, held to be living there still.
The unstruck music (anhad) sounds within in the encounter with the Lord.
Light is seen without sun or moon in the sky of the head.
At Sahasdal Kanwal the sounds of bell and conch; a flame of light (Jot Nirañjan).
The sārangī in Sunn, the flute at Bhanwar Guphā, the vīṇā in Sach Khand.
At the eye centre stars, then a moon and a sun are seen; then the radiant form of the master appears within.
At the initiate's death the master's radiant form comes to receive the soul.
At Trikuṭī a sound like thunder or the drum (mṛdaṅg), with the red sun of Brahm.
Nectar rains or drips in the sky-circle of the head.
The state of śānta: neither pain nor pleasure, neither hatred nor envy, equal toward all beings; the natural state from which all emotions arise and into which they return.
Looking and looking at the sky-like nature, seeing ceases.
Sarvānanda at Mehar saw all ten Mahāvidyās one after another in a single night (the tradition's account).
The eight involuntary bodily signs of strong feeling: paralysis, sweat, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of colour, tears and fainting.
Union (sāyujya) with the Goddess granted at the mere words 'Bhavāni tvam' (SL 22).
When Kuṇḍalinī unites with Śiva in the thousand-petalled lotus, the nectar of their union and the bliss called liberation arise.
For those in whom light has dawned and whose minds are undisturbed, knowledge of past and future is like perception.
Dreams of the seen, heard, experienced, longed-for, imagined, portending and doṣa-born.
When Shandao recited, a ray of light issued from his mouth at each recitation, ten or a hundred for ten or a hundred recitations (the tradition's account).

The five experiences of calm abiding: movement (like a waterfall off a cliff), attainment (like a river in a gorge), familiarity (like a gently flowing river), stability (like an ocean without waves) and perfection (like a mountain / steady flame).
notes: Similes vary between texts; given from memory.

description: At dawn on the ninety-fifth day of his retreat at the Rokkakudō (1201) Prince Shōtoku / Kannon appeared to Shinran in a dream with a verse, after which he went to Hōnen.
Showering rapture breaks over the body again and again like waves on the sea-shore.
At liberation the soul rises in one instant, straight up, like a flame or a gourd freed of its clay, and abides at the summit of the universe in its own knowledge and bliss.
Bhusuku and Maṇibhadrā rise into the air (the lives, from memory).
The perfected one does not notice whether his body sits or rises, like one intoxicated with his garment; the body continues while its karma lasts.
The tradition holds that the Siddhars remain present in their samādhi shrines and hill retreats and appear to devotees.
The perfected yogin is not stained by action or by sin.
The eight powers Aṇimā and the rest attend the Goddess at the outer gate and are rays of her own body; the gods won their powers only by waiting there (SL 93, 96).
Not seeing the path of the gods, the pole-star, Venus, the moon's shadow or Arundhatī: death within a year; further signs with shorter spans.

Relief of pain, normal voice and complexion, growth, strength, appetite, good digestion, timely sleep, absence of morbid dreams, easy waking, free passage of wastes and unimpaired mind, intellect and senses.
notes: Ca Vi 8.89 checked in the DCS e-text; no separate teaching entry.

description: Signs that power has descended: devotion to Śiva, the desire for release, detachment and faith in the teacher (list low confidence).
Disappearing, recollection, radiance, far sight and hearing, entering another body and creating objects at will are the signs of yogic success.

queries: local text at the stated ref
checks.note: YS 3.202–203 has 'antardhānaṃ smṛtiḥ kāntir dṛṣṭiḥ śrotrajñatā tathā | nijaṃ śarīram utsṛjya parakāyapraveśanam || arthānāṃ chandataḥ sṛṣṭir yogasiddher hi lakṣaṇam'.

description: Tears, a choked voice and horripilation while taking the name, longed for as the sign of love.
The sages see Śiva dancing with Viṣṇu in the sky, a treasury of splendour, whom the devoted see as light.
The bliss of the world is the joy of samādhi.

Production of bodies, joining and separating elements, assembling the universe, mastery of the wheel of powers; mastery of the elements (3.5) - with the warning that powers under the veil of delusion are not liberation (3.6).
Wonder (vismaya) marks the stages of yoga.
Superknowledges born of the fourth dhyāna: magical power (movement swift as mind, creation), divine ear, others' minds, former lives, death and rebirth, destruction of outflows.
Each of the six teachers claims to be an arahant with powers to win the sandalwood bowl; Piṇḍola flies up and takes it, and the Buddha forbids display of powers to lay people.
In sleep the breaths go into the self and one knows nothing by mind, speech, smell, sight or hearing.

description: All colours become one colour; 'I' and 'you' are gone.
From the unmeṣa arise quickly light, sound, form and taste, agitating the embodied - read as a caution.
For the yogin resting in spanda, desired objects are accomplished in waking and clearly revealed in dream.
In extreme anger, great joy, perplexity or running, the state reached is where spanda is established.
Resting in spanda, in- and out-breath set in the suṣumnā and rise beyond the cosmic egg; in that great space the deluded are as in deep sleep, the awakened unveiled.
Success or failure in song depends on the petal on which the jīva rests; dwelling in the brahmarandhra, bathed in nectar, the singer accomplishes music excellently.

Nāda arises when the self, wishing to speak, moves the mind, the mind strikes the body's fire and the fire drives the wind up from the knot of Brahmā through navel, heart, throat and head to the mouth, taking five forms from very subtle to artificial.

When the jīva dwells on the petals of the body's centres, particular states arise — e.g. in the moon centre compassion, forbearance, uprightness, fortitude, dispassion, steadiness, joy, laughter, horripilation, tears of meditation, stability, depth, effort, clarity, generosity, one-pointedness.
With calm, pliancy of mind arises, then of body; a lightness is felt (as if in the head) spreading through the body; the unwieldiness of body and mind is removed.
In the beginning stage the body becomes harmonious, fragrant, lustrous, the voice perfected; strong digestion, happiness, beauty, fullness of heart, strength.
With the tongue at the root of the palate and attention on the pit of the throat, hunger and thirst cease; attention on the kūrma-channel below it gives great steadiness of mind.

The first inner sound is like intoxicated bees, flute and vīṇā; then like a bell; then like the rumble of clouds; setting the mind fearlessly on it, laya arises and the mind is stilled with the sound.
In paricaya the breath stays in the space of suṣumnā, pierces the centres, and the yogin sees the 'three peaks' of his karma.
Sweat, then trembling, then hopping like a frog, then leaving the ground in padmāsana; little sleep and excreta; no sweat, saliva or worms; freedom from disease.
After gazing at one's shadow in bright sun, one's own image is seen in the sky; seeing it whole is a sign of long life and victory.

When the six openings are closed with the fingers and the breath restrained, the yogin sees the self as light; whoever sees it even for a moment is freed of sins; by constant practice he forgets the body and becomes one with it.
The bliss born of a moment of non-dual contemplation, not obtained by enjoyers in a crore of years.
One united with Śiva no longer sees the net of the world; the ocean of māyā dissolves in the submarine fire of oneness.
The yogin abides in a heart empty of mental activity, dissolved in Śiva and untroubled.
The inner liṅga is seen gold at the base, coral-red in the heart and crystal-clear between the brows.
The heart-shrine is touched by the inner breath and cooled by nectar dripping from the moon at the crown.
The prāṇaliṅga appears as a light rising from the navel-bulb when prāṇa and apāna meet; the breath dissolves in it like frost in the sun; within the yogin it shines like a lamp.
Above the brows the thousand-petalled lotus with a stainless moon-disc, within it a subtle aperture called Kailāsa where Śambhu is contemplated.
Marks of the Śivayogin: seeing the world as consciousness, desire and anger conquered, clod, stone and gold equal, friend and foe equal, free of longing and ego.
When the knot is broken in the sthirā view, all worldly activity appears to the wise like children playing at houses of dust.

Sthūlabhadra, having learned the Pūrvas, took the form of a lion to show his power to his visiting sisters; Bhadrabāhu judged him unfit and withheld the meaning of the last four Pūrvas — the tradition's warning that displaying powers costs the teaching.
Suffering brings the loss of pride, compassion for those in saṃsāra, shrinking from evil and longing for the Victor.
Śuka rises by yoga from the peak of Kailāsa into the sky and passes beyond, while the mountains and trees answer Vyāsa's cry.
The yoginī Sulabhā, versed in yoga, enters king Janaka's understanding 'sattva by sattva'.
Intense bodily pain arising in long unmoving sits is watched with strong mindfulness until it breaks up and subsides.
Fifty states — lights, visions of buddhas, sudden grief or boldness, elation, false nirvāṇas — as the aggregates are penetrated; to be recognized and not taken as sagehood.
In a dream the guru Bābājī places a hand on Tukārām's head and gives the mantra 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari'.
When the fivefold quality of yoga (earth, water, fire, wind, space) arises, there is no sickness, old age or death for one who has gained a body made of the fire of yoga.
